title: Canonical scalar augmentation to a strict coefficient-tower cone descends
statement: Let $R\to S$ be a map of commutative ring sheaves on a small site. Let $(B_n)_{n\geq1}$ be a strict inverse sequence of commutative $S$-algebras with $S$-linear transition maps, and assume countable products of $S$-module sheaves are exact. For a complex $P$ of $R$-modules put $F(P)=P\otimes_R S$ and $G(P)=\operatorname{Cone}(1-s:\prod_n\operatorname{Res}^S_{B_n}(P\otimes_R B_n)\to\prod_n\operatorname{Res}^S_{B_n}(P\otimes_R B_n))[-1]$, using restriction of scalars [def-pc-sheaf-restrict-scalars] and module-derived categories [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category, def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. There is a unique chain natural transformation $\beta:F\to G$ whose product projections send $p\otimes s$ to $p\otimes\bar s$ and whose shifted-product component is zero. The notation $\bar s$ means the image of $s$ in $B_n$, without a surjectivity assumption. On flat-term K-flat representatives [def-pc-kflat-complex], $F,G$ compute their everywhere-defined left derived functors $LF,LG$, and $\beta$ descends uniquely to $\chi:LF\to LG$ normalized by their universal comparison isomorphisms on those representatives. Thus $\chi$ is natural on the entire derived category and independent of the representative. For $S=R$ and $B_n=R/a^nR$, multiplication $P\otimes_R R\cong P$ identifies $\beta_P$ with the quotient unit having zero shifted-product component. All tensor products of module sheaves are sheafified tensor products [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product], applied termwise to complexes when an ordinary tensor is written.

source.place: Definition 3.4.10 and Proposition 3.5.1, pp. 22,24: completion via derived reduction towers. Explicit scalar augmentation and resolving-class descent are expanded here; not a verbatim assertion of the source.

proof.text: Use the ordinary extension functor in the cochain derived-change-of-rings model for R to S. Apply the compatible coefficient-tower theorem to r_n = phi followed by c_n and p_n = c_n. Its level presentations, additive structure, map formulas and transition formulas give the required ScalarTowerTensorModel. The scalar commutativity hypothesis follows by associativity from c_(n+1) followed by b_n = c_n.

source.place: Tags 06YY and 03EK; the existing cochain model and compatible coefficient tower

proof.text: Write $c_n:S\to B_n$ and $t_n:B_{n+1}\to B_n$ for the structure and transition maps of the strict tower of $S$-algebras; thus $t_nc_{n+1}=c_n$. For every degree of $P$, the balanced map $p\otimes s\mapsto p\otimes c_n(s)$ defines an $S$-linear map $\alpha_{n,P}:P\otimes_RS\to\operatorname{Res}^S_{B_n}(P\otimes_RB_n)$. Indeed, $rp\otimes c_n(s)=p\otimes c_n(\varphi(r)s)$ for a local section $r$ of $R$. These presheaf maps commute with restriction and therefore induce maps on the sheafified tensor products. The identity $t_nc_{n+1}=c_n$ implies $(1\otimes t_n)\alpha_{n+1,P}=\alpha_{n,P}$. The product universal property gives a unique $\alpha_P:F(P)\to V(P)=\prod_n\operatorname{Res}^S_{B_n}(P\otimes_RB_n)$ with these components, and $(1-s_P)\alpha_P=0$.

source.place: Section Tag 03EK (section-tensor-product); explicit balanced scalar map

proof.text: Use the fixed strict Roos coordinates $G(P)^i=V(P)^{i-1}\oplus V(P)^i$, with $d(y,x)=(-dy-(1-s_P)x,dx)$. Define $\beta_P(z)=(0,\alpha_P(z))$. Since $\alpha_P$ commutes with differentials and $(1-s_P)\alpha_P=0$, its differential is $(0,\alpha_P(dz))$, so this is a chain map. For a chain map $f:P\to P'$, every product projection of $V(f)\alpha_P$ and $\alpha_{P'}F(f)$ sends $p\otimes s$ to $f(p)\otimes c_n(s)$; hence these maps agree and $G(f)\beta_P=\beta_{P'}F(f)$. Any map with zero first component and the stipulated product projections has second component $\alpha_P$ by the product universal property. Pure tensors locally generate the sheafified tensors, so the stipulated formulas determine the maps even when sections are not globally pure tensors. This proves the chain-level existence, uniqueness, and naturality.

The ordinary functor $F$ sends a chain homotopy $h$ to $h\otimes1$. For the tensor tower, its levelwise homotopies are $h\otimes1_{B_n}$; they commute with transitions because $(h\otimes1)(1\otimes t_n)=(1\otimes t_n)(h\otimes1)$. The strict Roos homotopy lemma therefore sends them to the homotopy $(y,x)\mapsto(-h_Vy,h_Vx)$, where $h_V=\prod_n(h\otimes1_{B_n})$. Thus both functors pass to the homotopy category of $R$-module complexes, and then to functors $\overline F,\overline G:K(R)\to D(S)$ by localization in the target. Their chain-natural transformation gives $\overline\beta:\overline F\to\overline G$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be the homotopy-category objects represented by K-flat complexes with flat terms. Every unbounded $R$-module complex admits a quasi-isomorphism $P\to X$ with $P\in\mathcal P$, by the K-flat resolution theorem. Since the site is small, $\operatorname{Mod}(R)$ is abelian. Quasi-isomorphisms in $K(R)$ have right calculus of fractions and two-out-of-three, by the saturated multiplicative-system theorem. These are exactly the resolution and fraction hypotheses needed for resolving-class descent; no boundedness or projectivity assumption is introduced.

Apply the preservation clause of the cochain derived-change-of-rings model to each composite R to B_n. The level presentations form a natural isomorphism: their naturality follows by sheafification extensionality and the generator formula for V.map. The compatible coefficient-tower theorem states that restriction of scalars preserves and reflects quasi-isomorphisms. Transporting through the natural level isomorphisms therefore proves that V sends quasi-isomorphisms between K-flat complexes to levelwise quasi-isomorphisms. The ordinary R to S functor is already the one from its derived model.

source.place: Tag 06YT (lemma-derived-tor-quasi-isomorphism-other-side), with each coefficient ring in degree zero

proof.text: Exactness of countable products in $\operatorname{Mod}(S)$ gives $H^i(\prod_n C_n)=\prod_n H^i(C_n)$ for every family of complexes: the product functor preserves kernels and images, and applying it to $0\to\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}\to\ker d^i\to H^i\to0$ identifies the quotient. Consequently the product $V(f)$ of the restricted levelwise quasi-isomorphisms from the preceding step is a quasi-isomorphism. It commutes with $1-s$ because $f\otimes1$ is a strict tower map.

Exact products make the product map a quasi-isomorphism, by HomologicalComplex.quasiIso_limMap. The strict tower map yields a morphism of the two mapping-cone triangles. Localize those triangles; the first two vertical arrows are isomorphisms, hence the third is an isomorphism by the triangulated two-out-of-three lemma. Thus the cone map is a quasi-isomorphism, and shifting by minus one proves the assertion for the actual roosF map. This uses the fixed cone directly, without changing coordinates.

Apply resolving-class essential constancy to $K(R)$, its quasi-isomorphisms, the class $\mathcal P$, and each of $\overline F,\overline G$. The preceding steps verify every hypothesis. For each $X$ the denominator diagram is essentially constant, and for $X\in\mathcal P$ its identity leg is invertible. The pointwise-Kan bridge identifies this cone with a pointwise right Kan extension along $Q_R:K(R)\to D(R)$ and identifies the identity leg with the universal comparison. The total-left-derived-localization theorem assembles these pointwise extensions into everywhere-defined left derived functors $LF,LG:D(R)\to D(S)$ with comparisons $\varepsilon_F:LFQ_R\to\overline F$ and $\varepsilon_G:LGQ_R\to\overline G$. Both comparisons are isomorphisms on $\mathcal P$. This also shows directly that the actual ordinary tensor and product-cone models compute these functors on the stated representatives.

source.place: Tag 06XN (lemma-find-existence-computes), dual argument, and Tag 05S9 (definition-right-derived-functor-defined); the pointwise Kan formulation is the cited bridge

proof.text: Compose $LFQ_R\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_F}\overline F\xrightarrow{\overline\beta}\overline G$. By the universal property of the right Kan extension $(LG,\varepsilon_G)$ there is a unique natural transformation $\chi:LF\to LG$ satisfying $\varepsilon_{G,X}\chi_{Q_RX}=\overline\beta_X\varepsilon_{F,X}$ for every $X\in K(R)$. For $P\in\mathcal P$, invert the comparison to obtain precisely $\chi_{Q_RP}=\varepsilon_{G,P}^{-1}Q_S(\beta_P)\varepsilon_{F,P}$. This constructs a transformation on the entire derived category, rather than only a family of maps on chosen resolutions.

source.place: Universal property of a left derived functor/right Kan extension; cf. Tag 05S9

proof.text: The normalization alone determines $\chi$. For any complex $X$ choose the quasi-isomorphism $q:P\to X$ of the K-flat resolution theorem. Since $Q_Rq$ is invertible, naturality forces $\chi_{Q_RX}=LG(Q_Rq)\chi_{Q_RP}LF(Q_Rq)^{-1}$. Thus two normalized natural transformations coincide on every localized complex, and hence on every derived object. The transformation already constructed satisfies this formula for every resolution, so changing the resolution gives the same map under the canonical comparisons. Changing models of $LF$ or $LG$ also gives the same transformation after their comparison-preserving universal isomorphisms, by uniqueness of universal objects. The K-flat resolution theorem presents flatness using the monoidal tensor functor; siteSheafTensorRightIso from the independent-coefficient tensor-colimits theorem transports that exactness to IsFlatOnSite.

source.place: Tag 06YS (lemma-K-flat-resolution); uniqueness from invertibility of the localized resolution

proof.text: Finally set $S=R$ and $B_n=R/a^nR$, with the usual quotient transition maps and $a$ a global section of $R$. Multiplication $m:P\otimes_RR\to P$, $p\otimes r\mapsto rp$, has inverse $p\mapsto p\otimes1$; both formulas respect restriction and hence sheafification. The $n$th projection of $\beta_Pm^{-1}$ is $p\mapsto p\otimes\overline1$, and its shifted-product component is zero. These are exactly the projections and zero component of the quotient unit in the strict Roos definition, so the two chain maps agree. The formulas also cover $a=0$ (constant tower $R$) and $a$ invertible (zero quotient tower).

source.place: Definition 3.4.10 and Proposition 3.5.1, pp. 22,24; explicit quotient-unit normalization

proof_origin.place: Definition 3.4.10 and Proposition 3.5.1 give the completion context. The Lean proof constructs the model with the existing cochain scalar-extension model and compatible coefficient tower, constructs the scalar maps by sheafification of sectionwise balanced maps, and uses the strict Roos homotopy factorization. Exact-product cone invariance and resolving-class pointwise Kan extension give descent; the quotient-unit formula follows from the explicit identity-scalar multiplication isomorphism. Source: Stacks 03EK, 014E, 08TC, 06YS, 06YT, 06XN and 05S9.
